blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Video world models aim to create interactive physical worlds that capture how diverse materials move and interact. Yet material-dependent dynamics remain underexplored in controllable video generation, limiting reliable control in scenes with different materials. We present WorldInteract, a streaming video generation framework that decomposes cross-material interaction into material-dependent behavior generation and contact response computation. External pushes and contact impulses are expressed through a shared velocity-increment interface, allowing material behaviors learned from interaction-free videos to be reused in interacting scenes. A physics controller predicts contacts and computes velocity increments from estimated masses and restitution coefficients, while a causal generator executes these increments using learned material behaviors. This separation enables cross-material interaction without supervised contact videos spanning diverse material pairings and contact configurations. We train the generator on 30k simulated interaction-free videos spanning 22 material classes and introduce Material-Aware RL, using verifiable physical rewards to refine material behavior and control execution. WorldInteract substantially outperforms state-of-the-art methods on Physics-IQ and delivers more reliable push control on real-world images.
blocks.zh: 视频世界模型旨在创造互动物理世界,捕捉出不同材料如何移动和互动. 然而,依赖材料的动态在可控视频生成方面仍然没有得到充分利用,限制了对不同材料的场景的可靠控制. 我们介绍World Interact,一个流动的视频生成框架,将跨材料交互分解成依赖材料的行为生成和接触响应计算. 外推和接触冲动通过共享速度-增量界面来表达,使得从无互动视频中吸取的物质行为可以在互动场景中被再用. 物理控制器会预测接触并从估计质量和还原系数中计算出速度递增,而因果发生器则利用所学的材料行为执行这些递增. 这种分离可以实现跨材料交互,而无需监督的接触视频,涵盖不同的材料配对和接触配置。 我们训练发电机使用30k模拟无相互作用视频,这些视频跨越22个材料类,并采用材料-Aware RL,利用可核查的物理奖励来完善材料行为和控制执行. blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Interactive video world models aim to respond to user actions with
physically plausible outcomes, yet the same push can roll a ball, slide a
box, or scatter a pile of sand. Mass and friction affect how far an object travels after a push; mass and restitution govern how contact
changes the motion of both objects. Reliable control therefore requires modeling both material behavior , which describes how an object moves under an applied velocity change, and contact response , which determines how momentum is exchanged when objects collide. Their combination governs cross-material interactions. Ignoring either component makes control unreliable when materials or contact partners change.

Learning these behaviors directly from contact videos creates a coverage
problem. Adding a material introduces new pairings with existing materials,
even if its individual behavior is already represented. Each pairing can
also appear under different contact configurations. Supervision must cover
these combinations as well as individual material behaviors, making it
costly to extend control to new materials.

configurations.

blocks.en:
We construct 30k simulated interaction-free videos , which contain no
object–object contact, spanning 22 material classes. Scene memory maintains
spatial state and object identity as generation proceeds under updated
controls. Supervised video reconstruction alone does not directly enforce
relative material behaviors or the timing of control events. We introduce Material-Aware RL to refine material behavior and control execution
through verifiable physical rewards on generated rollouts. These rollouts
include contact scenes produced with the physics controller, extending
training beyond the interaction-free supervision. Experiments demonstrate clear
advantages over state-of-the-art methods, with stronger physical consistency
on Physics-IQ and higher push success on real-world images.

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Motion-conditioned video models guide objects through spatial controls.
DragAnything [ 36 ] , Tora [ 40 ] , and
FlashMotion [ 19 ] generate motion along specified
trajectories, while DragStream [ 41 ] and
MotionStream [ 29 ] allow motion guidance to change
during streaming generation. Such controls specify desired motion, but do
not by themselves determine how material properties and contact alter that
motion. WorldInteract uses velocity increments as physical inputs, leaving
material behavior to the generator and contact response computation to the
physics controller.

the latter online reduces the need for supervision over material pairings

blocks.en:
This stage learns to preserve material-dependent behavior while accepting
new interactions during streaming generation. Scene memory records the

Starting from the Stage-1 checkpoint, we replace full attention with

first frame as z 0 z_{0} and each subsequent four-frame chunk as z ℓ z_{\ell} .

We represent scene state with two maps: c pos c^{\mathrm{pos}} records 3D
positions derived from Depth-Anything-3 [ 20 ] , and c trk c^{\mathrm{trk}} assigns each object a persistent identity using
SAM2 [ 28 ] . Both maps are updated from each decoded chunk, providing

3.3 Material-Aware RL
blocks.zh: 3.3 材料-软件RL

blocks.en:
Flow matching does not directly enforce physical relations such as
stronger pushes producing greater displacement. Material-Aware RL uses
verifiable rewards on generated rollouts to refine material behavior
and velocity-increment execution.

可核查地奖励产生的推出,以完善物质行为
和速度递增的处决。

blocks.en:
We use simulated pairs that vary only in material or push magnitude,
real-world image pairs with different push magnitudes, and simulated
initial scenes with objects on a collision course. For each input, we
sample K = 4 K=4 rollouts. In contact scenes, the controller supplies velocity
increments for predicted contacts, providing interaction experience without
supervised contact videos.

SAM2 masks, CoTracker3 [ 15 ] tracks, and depth maps provide
four checks: displacement accuracy ( r disp r_{\mathrm{disp}} ), agreement with
requested velocity increments ( r Δ ​ v r_{\Delta v} ), relative behavior across
paired inputs ( r rel r_{\mathrm{rel}} ), and event timing ( r sync r_{\mathrm{sync}} ).
Simulated interaction-free inputs provide target displacements. For real-world
images and contact scenes, displacement is scored only for objects
receiving no increment, rewarding unaffected neighbors that stay still.
Contact execution is evaluated against the controller’s increments,
so the rewards train the generator to follow a contact response while
the controller remains responsible for computing it.

( Tab. 1 ), 15 points above the strongest baseline, Goal Force,
even though Goal Force uses a much larger backbone.
The IoU components explain the gain. On spatial IoU, which checks only where motion happens, Goal Force
is close to our model. On spatiotemporal IoU, which
also checks when it happens, our model scores more than twice as high as any baseline. Both models move objects to similar places, but ours moves them at the right time.

Our model keeps each pushed object intact and resolves the contact

blocks.en: 5 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 5 结论

blocks.en:
We presented WorldInteract, a streaming video generation framework that
combines material-dependent behavior generation with contact response
computation through a shared
velocity-increment interface. Interaction-free videos teach reusable material behavior, causal training with scene memory maintains spatial state and
object identity, and Material-Aware RL improves the execution of physical
controls on generated rollouts. A physics controller composes contact
responses from object properties estimated by a VLM, allowing supervised
data to focus on individual materials without enumerating every material
pairing and contact configuration. The existing evaluations on Physics-IQ
and real images support the effectiveness of this decomposition for
physical accuracy and control adherence. The current controller uses
approximate geometry and a frictionless central collision model; extending
the same interface to richer contact models is a direction for future work.

blocks.en:
Flow matching scores each clip in isolation and weighs all pixels equally,
so small physical errors, such as a drifting neighbor or a velocity change
one frame early, cost little, and relations such as a harder push
traveling farther are never compared. Stage 3 therefore samples rollouts
from the current model, including rollouts with controller-generated
contacts, scores them with verifiable checkers, and increases the relative
likelihood of rollouts that satisfy them. During Stage 3, the controller
uses simulator properties for simulated inputs and VLM estimates
precomputed offline for real images, so no VLM runs inside the training
loop.

blocks.en:
Figure S1 shows six scenes in which a pushed object
strikes a second object, in most cases of a different material: a steel
bottle and a knitted pouf, two wooden blocks, a brick and a bean bag, a
stone and a foam block, a wooden cube and a plastic toy bin, and a wooden
box and a cushion.
The failure modes identified in the main paper recur across all six scenes.
Wan2.2 adds content instead of executing the push: a hand, a foot, or a pair
of legs enters the frame in three scenes, the pouf swells until it fills the
view, and the wooden box tumbles and breaks apart. Force Prompting leaves the
pushed object nearly in place, and StreamForce moves it only slightly, so in
both cases the contact described by the prompt never occurs. Goal Force
produces motion but violates rigid-body behavior: the brick splits in two,
the foam block and the wooden cube deform, the wooden box collapses into a
wedge, and the pouf dissolves into colored artifacts. Our model moves each
pushed object along the push until it reaches the target and keeps both
objects intact through the contact.

blocks.en:
Figures S2 and S3 show six streaming rollouts with
four to five pushes each. Pushes are issued while generation is in progress,
often to an object that has already moved, and a single rollout can involve
several objects of different materials, e.g . , an apple, a cast-iron pot, a
copper saucepan, and a heap of flour on the same counter. The three
baselines fail in distinct ways. RealWonder simulates reconstructed 3D
geometry, so reconstruction errors become visible as soon as an object
moves: the tissue box folds into an open tray, the mug shatters into flat
discs and disappears, the sled turns into a green boat, the apple splits,
and the winter table fills with objects that were never in the input, such as a toy plane and glowing rings. FlashMotion keeps every scene essentially static. StreamForce moves some objects but accumulates error over the rollout, with haze, loss of contrast and texture, and ghosted objects by the
final frames. Our model executes each push at the object’s current position,
produces both rigid sliding and the spreading of granular flour and snow,
and preserves the appearance of the scene for the full rollout.
